fourier-optics-001.question: Which is the correct spatial frequency of sinusoidal bright and dark fringes with a period of 2 µm?
choices: 0.5 cycles/mm
About 3.1×10³ cycles/mm
500 cycles/mm
fourier-optics-001.explanation: Spatial frequency is the number of periods per unit length, the reciprocal of the period. The period is 2 µm = 2×10⁻³ mm, so 1/(2×10⁻³ mm) = 500 cycles/mm. 0.5 cycles/mm mistakes 1/(2 µm) = 0.5 µm⁻¹ for mm⁻¹. About 3.1×10³ cycles/mm is the angular spatial frequency 2π/d, multiplied by 2π; its unit is rad/mm, and it is not a count of periods. In Fourier optics, any distribution of brightness is treated as a superposition of sinusoidal fringes with various spatial frequencies and orientations. The MTF that describes lens performance and the Nyquist frequency of an image sensor are also compared in units of cycles/mm (lp/mm).

fourier-optics-002.question: Using an aberration-free convex lens of focal length f, you want the exact Fourier transform (with no extra phase factor) of the amplitude distribution of a transmitting object illuminated with collimated coherent light. Which arrangement of the object and observation plane is correct?
choices: Place the object in contact just in front of the lens and observe just behind the lens
Place the object in the front focal plane of the lens and observe in the back focal plane of the lens
Place the object 2f in front of the lens and observe in the plane 2f behind it
fourier-optics-002.explanation: Within the paraxial range, the amplitude in the back focal plane of a lens is the Fourier transform of the object's amplitude distribution, and the component of spatial frequency ν gathers at position x = λfν. Placing the object in the front focal plane cancels the extra quadratic phase factor, giving an exact Fourier transform in both amplitude and phase (with the object just in front of the lens, the intensity distribution in the back focal plane is the same, but a quadratic phase factor remains). Just behind the lens, the light still has almost the same distribution as the object, and it is not a Fourier transform. The 2f–2f arrangement forms an inverted image at unit magnification, which corresponds to applying the Fourier transform twice, not to the object's Fourier transform.

fourier-optics-003.question: A sinusoidal amplitude grating with a spatial frequency of 100 cycles/mm is placed in the front focal plane of a lens with a focal length of 200 mm and illuminated with collimated light of wavelength 633 nm. Which is closest to the distance from the optical axis of the points where the ±1st diffracted orders gather in the back focal plane? (Use the paraxial approximation.)
choices: About 12.7 mm
About 79.5 mm
About 1.27 mm
fourier-optics-003.explanation: The component of spatial frequency ν is diffracted in the direction sinθ = λν and gathers at x = λfν in the back focal plane. x = 633×10⁻⁶ mm × 200 mm × 100 mm⁻¹ ≈ 12.7 mm (θ ≈ 3.6°, so the paraxial approximation holds). About 79.5 mm multiplies by an extra 2π, confusing spatial frequency with angular spatial frequency. About 1.27 mm is off by a factor of ten in converting from nm to mm. A sinusoidal amplitude grating produces only three points, the zeroth and ±1st orders, and higher-frequency components gather farther from the axis. Using this relationship, you can read off an object's spatial frequencies from positions in the focal plane, or block only specific frequency components.

fourier-optics-004.question: A 4f system is built with two lenses of focal lengths f₁ = 100 mm and f₂ = 200 mm (the object in the front focal plane of the first lens, and the lens separation f₁ + f₂). Which correctly pairs the lateral magnification of the image and the total length from object to image?
choices: Magnification −2 (inverted), total length 300 mm
Magnification −2 (inverted), total length 600 mm
Magnification −0.5 (inverted), total length 600 mm
fourier-optics-004.explanation: In a 4f system, the first lens forms the Fourier transform of the object in the shared focal plane (the Fourier plane), and the second lens Fourier-transforms it again to form an image in its back focal plane. Applying the Fourier transform twice reverses the coordinates, so the image is inverted, with lateral magnification −f₂/f₁ = −200/100 = −2. The total length is f₁ + (f₁ + f₂) + f₂ = 2f₁ + 2f₂ = 600 mm. 300 mm counts only the separation between the two lenses. A magnification of −0.5 inverts the ratio of focal lengths. Because a 4f system lets you manipulate spatial-frequency components directly in the Fourier plane and is telecentric on both the object and image sides, it is used for spatial filtering, pattern recognition and pulse shaping.

fourier-optics-005.question: A small opaque stop that blocks only the zeroth-order light is placed at the center (on the optical axis) of the Fourier plane of a 4f system. Which correctly describes the change in the image of an object illuminated with coherent light?
choices: The uniform-brightness component is removed, so the background turns dark and the object's edges and fine structures stand out brightly
The center is where the fine-structure components gather, so they are removed and the whole image becomes smoothly blurred
The zeroth order only sets the average brightness, so the image just dims uniformly and its shapes and contrast do not change
fourier-optics-005.explanation: In the Fourier plane, the uniform-brightness component (zero spatial frequency) gathers on the optical axis, and finer-structure components lie farther out. Blocking only the center acts as a high-pass spatial filter that removes low-frequency components, leaving only edges where brightness changes and fine structures in the image, so the outlines are emphasized. Since the specimen's structures glow on a dark background, it is the same idea as darkfield illumination in a microscope. Blurring by removing fine structure happens in the opposite case, with a pinhole that passes only the center (a low-pass filter). Blocking the zeroth order changes the proportions of the components, so it does not simply lower the brightness uniformly. Shifting only the phase of the zeroth order gives the principle of the phase-contrast microscope.

fourier-optics-006.question: A laser-beam spatial filter consists of a pinhole placed at the focus of a lens that focuses the beam. Which correctly describes what the pinhole does?
choices: Passing through the pinhole narrows the beam's spectral width, so the monochromaticity of the laser light improves and interference fringes gain contrast
The smaller the pinhole compared with the focal spot, the more diffraction smooths the wavefront, so the cleanup improves without any loss of output power
The focus is the beam's Fourier plane; disturbances from dirt or nonuniformity have high spatial frequencies and spread around the focus, so the pinhole blocks them and smooths the beam
fourier-optics-006.explanation: The focal plane of the focusing lens is the Fourier plane of the incoming beam's amplitude distribution. An ideal Gaussian beam forms a small spot at the focus, but fine disturbances from dirt or scratches on lenses and from beam nonuniformity are high-spatial-frequency components, so they spread around the focus. Placing a pinhole slightly larger than the spot blocks only the disturbance components, and the beam recollimated by a lens approaches a smooth Gaussian. The 1/e² diameter of the focal spot is about 4λf/(πD); with a wavelength of 633 nm, f = 10 mm and a beam diameter of 2 mm it is about 4 µm, so as a guide a pinhole of about 1.5 times that diameter is used. A pinhole smaller than the spot clips even the center of the beam and loses much of the power. The pinhole selects a spatial distribution and does not change the spectral width.

fourier-optics-007.question: An aberration-free circular aperture is changed to an annular aperture by blocking a concentric central region (such as the central obstruction from the secondary mirror of a reflecting telescope). With the outer diameter unchanged, which correctly describes the change in the point image in the focal plane?
choices: The bright central part widens and the surrounding rings disappear, giving a point image close to a Gaussian
The width of the bright central part becomes slightly narrower, but the fraction of energy going into the surrounding rings increases
Because the outer diameter is the same, only the brightness decreases and the shape of the point image does not change
fourier-optics-007.explanation: The amplitude of the point image is the Fourier transform of the pupil function (the amplitude distribution of the aperture), and its intensity is the squared magnitude of that. Blocking the center increases the share of the outer part of the pupil, making high-spatial-frequency components relatively stronger, so the bright central part (the Airy disk) becomes slightly narrower. In exchange, energy moves into the surrounding rings, and the MTF falls at intermediate frequencies. A widening central part with disappearing rings is the effect of apodization, which lowers the transmittance toward the edge of the aperture, the opposite direction. Even with the same outer diameter, changing the pupil's shape changes its Fourier transform, the point image, so the option saying only the brightness decreases is also wrong.

fourier-optics-008.question: Which correctly pairs the condition under which diffraction by an aperture can be treated as Fraunhofer diffraction (the amplitude of the diffraction pattern at the observation plane is the Fourier transform of the aperture's amplitude distribution) and a way to achieve it over a short distance? (a is the aperture radius, L the distance to the observation plane and λ the wavelength.)
choices: When the Fresnel number a²/(λL) is much larger than 1; observing in the focal plane of a lens gives the same diffraction pattern even at a short distance
When the aperture is much larger than the wavelength and light travels straight as in geometric optics; the shadow of the aperture itself becomes the diffraction pattern
When the Fresnel number a²/(λL) is much smaller than 1; observing in the focal plane of a lens gives the same diffraction pattern even at a short distance
fourier-optics-008.explanation: When the phase difference πa²/(λL) from the quadratic term in the distance from each point of the aperture to the observation point is negligible, that is, when the Fresnel number NF = a²/(λL) ≪ 1, the diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture's amplitude distribution. For an aperture of radius 1 mm at a wavelength of 500 nm, a²/λ = 2 m, so a distance well beyond that, tens of m or more, is needed. With a lens, collimated components traveling in the same direction gather at one point in the focal plane, bringing the diffraction pattern at infinity to the focal plane. When NF ≫ 1, only fine fringes appear at the edges of the aperture's shadow, and it is not Fraunhofer diffraction. A shadow cast as it is corresponds to the geometric-optics limit where diffraction is inconspicuous, and the Fourier-transform relationship does not hold. The region where NF is around 1 is treated as Fresnel diffraction.

fourier-optics-009.question: When collimated coherent light of wavelength 500 nm strikes a grating of period d = 10 µm at normal incidence, an image with the same bright and dark pattern as the grating, with no lateral shift, appears at a certain distance from the grating (the Talbot effect). Which is closest to this first distance (the Talbot distance zT = 2d²/λ, paraxial approximation)?
choices: About 0.4 mm
About 0.2 mm
About 0.1 mm
fourier-optics-009.explanation: The Talbot distance is zT = 2d²/λ = 2 × (10×10⁻⁶)² / (500×10⁻⁹) = 4×10⁻⁴ m, that is, about 0.4 mm. About 0.2 mm is zT/2; an image of the grating also appears there, but it is shifted laterally by half a period, so it does not meet the condition of an unshifted image. About 0.1 mm is zT/4, a position where the grating's image does not reappear: a sinusoidal amplitude grating shows weak fringes of half the period, and a rectangular grating with equal bright and dark parts gives uniform brightness. The light diffracted by a grating is a set of plane waves at fixed angles, and as it propagates the phase of each order shifts in proportion to the square of the order; every zT the phases of all orders line up again and the original distribution returns. Because images of periodic structures form without a lens, the effect is used for X-ray phase imaging, grating inspection and lithography.

fourier-optics-010.question: In holography, which correctly explains why a three-dimensional image of an object can be reconstructed from the recorded interference fringes?
choices: Interference fringes with the reference wave record both the amplitude and the phase of the object wave, and illuminating with the reference wave reproduces the original object wavefront by diffraction
The brightness distribution of the object is imaged with a lens and recorded like a photograph from two directions, one for each eye
The recording material is a special one that records the phase of the electric field directly rather than intensity, and depth is reproduced from that phase distribution
fourier-optics-010.explanation: Recording materials and image sensors can record only the intensity of light, and an ordinary photograph loses the phase information. In holography, a coherent reference wave R is superposed on the object wave O, and the intensity |O + R|² = |O|² + |R|² + OR* + O*R is recorded. The phase of O is written into the positions of the interference fringes, and the amplitude into their contrast. When the recorded hologram is illuminated with R, the transmitted light contains a component proportional to |R|²O, reproducing the very wavefront of the light that came from the object, so a three-dimensional image whose appearance changes with viewing direction is seen. Recording an image formed by a lens is ordinary photography. The recording material itself responds only to intensity; the phase is recorded after interference converts it into intensity fringes.

fourier-optics-011.question: A hologram is recorded with a He-Ne laser of wavelength 633 nm, with the object and reference waves crossing at an angle of 30°. Which is closest to the spacing of the recorded interference fringes? (Assume the two waves are incident symmetrically about the normal to the recording plane.)
choices: About 0.633 µm
About 2.45 µm
About 1.22 µm
fourier-optics-011.explanation: When two plane waves cross at an angle θ, the fringe spacing is Λ = λ/(2 sin(θ/2)). Λ = 633 nm / (2 × sin15°) = 633/(2 × 0.259) ≈ 1.22 µm, which as a spatial frequency is about 820 cycles/mm. About 0.633 µm uses the full angle instead of the half angle, giving λ/(2 sin30°). About 2.45 µm drops the factor 2 in the denominator, giving λ/sin(θ/2). Ordinary photographic film cannot record fringes this fine, so holograms use dedicated plates or photopolymers that can record several thousand cycles/mm. If the fringes move by even a fraction of their spacing during exposure the contrast is lost, so suppressing vibration of the optical table also matters.

fourier-optics-012.question: Compared with the in-line hologram first made by Gabor, in which the object and reference waves overlap on the same axis, which is the main advantage of the off-axis type (Leith–Upatnieks type), in which the reference wave enters at an angle?
choices: Bringing the reference wave in obliquely widens the fringe spacing, so even low-resolution photographic film can record it
On reconstruction, the object image, its conjugate (twin) image and the zeroth-order light separate into different directions and can be observed without overlapping
The object wave itself serves as the reference, so no separate reference wave is needed and even low-coherence light sources can be used
fourier-optics-012.explanation: The recorded intensity |O + R|² contains two terms, OR* and O*R, and on reconstruction the image of the object and a phase-reversed conjugate image (twin image) appear simultaneously. In the in-line type these two and the zeroth-order light overlap on the same axis, making the image hard to see. In the off-axis type the reference wave enters at an angle θ, so the image and conjugate image travel at ±θ from the direction of the reconstruction beam while the zeroth order continues along that direction, and they can be separated spatially. In exchange, when the object wave strikes the recording plane normally, the fringe spacing becomes as fine as about λ/sinθ, requiring high-resolution recording materials, so the option saying the fringes become wider has it backwards. Both types record phase through interference with the reference wave, so the reference wave is indispensable and the light source must be coherent.

fourier-optics-013.question: Which correctly explains why a reflection-type volume hologram (Denisyuk type), recorded with the object and reference waves entering the recording material from opposite sides, can reconstruct an image even under white-light illumination?
choices: Each wavelength in white light diffracts at a different angle, but within the thickness of a volume hologram the angular differences are corrected so the images of all colors overlap exactly
The fringe spacing is much larger than the recording wavelength and the diffraction angle is small, so all wavelengths diffract with the same efficiency and color shifts are hard to notice
Layered fringes form through the thickness at about half the wavelength in the material, and only colors near the recording wavelength satisfy the Bragg condition and are strongly reflected
fourier-optics-013.explanation: When two waves interfere head-on inside the material, fringes nearly parallel to the material's surface form in dozens of layers through its thickness, at a spacing of about half the wavelength in the material (λ/(2n)). This stack of layers acts like a dielectric multilayer mirror, reflecting only wavelengths that satisfy the Bragg condition, where the reflections from the layers reinforce. Even under white light, the image is therefore reconstructed only with a narrow band close to the recording wavelength, with little color smearing. In a thin transmission hologram, each wavelength of white light diffracts at a different angle, so images shifted in color overlap and smear. Volume holograms have strong wavelength and angle selectivity, so the option saying efficiency is independent of wavelength has it backwards. If the material shrinks during processing, the fringe spacing changes and the reconstructed color shifts from the recording wavelength.

fourier-optics-014.question: For a thin phase-type hologram (diffraction grating) whose phase varies sinusoidally, which is closest to the theoretical maximum first-order diffraction efficiency?
choices: About 34%
About 6.3%
fourier-optics-014.explanation: For a thin sinusoidal phase grating with phase amplitude a, the q-th order diffraction efficiency is expressed with Bessel functions as ηq = Jq²(a). The maximum of J₁ is about 0.582 at a ≈ 1.84, so the first-order efficiency is at most 0.582² ≈ 0.339, that is, about 34%. About 6.3% (1/16) is the first-order maximum for an amplitude grating whose transmittance varies sinusoidally, where much of the light is absorbed or goes into the zeroth order. 100% is a value achievable in principle with gratings having a sawtooth phase (blaze) or thick volume holograms satisfying the Bragg condition; with a thin sinusoidal phase grating the light also splits into higher orders, so it is not reached. Computer-generated holograms and spatial light modulators raise the efficiency by making the phase multilevel to approach a blaze.

fourier-optics-015.question: In digital holography, an off-axis hologram is recorded directly on an image sensor with a pixel pitch of 3.45 µm, with the object wave incident normally on the sensor and the reference wave at an angle θ (wavelength 633 nm). Which is the correct range of θ determined by the condition that one period of the interference fringes is sampled by at least 2 pixels?
choices: About 10.6° or less
About 5.3° or less
About 5.3° or more
fourier-optics-015.explanation: With the object wave at normal incidence and the reference wave at angle θ, the fringe period is λ/sinθ. Sampling it with at least 2 pixels requires λ/sinθ ≥ 2p, that is, sinθ ≤ λ/(2p) = 0.633/(2 × 3.45) ≈ 0.0917, so θ ≤ about 5.3°. About 10.6° or less comes from λ/sinθ ≥ p, receiving one period with one pixel, which fails the Nyquist condition so the fringes are not recorded correctly. The larger the angle, the finer the fringes, so the condition is an upper limit, and the option of about 5.3° or more has the direction reversed. On the other hand, too small an angle prevents the image from being separated from the zeroth order and the conjugate image in the reconstruction calculation, so the angle is chosen near the upper limit to suit the object's bandwidth. Image-sensor pixels are large, so the reference angle is limited to a few degrees or less.
